name: Fast Days for Rain (Taanit Geshamim)
notes: The structured progression of communal and individual fasts decreed when rain fails to fall, including the three stages of increasing severity

name: Prayer for Rain (Geshem / Tefillat Geshem)
notes: The insertion of rain-related phrases in the Amida (mashiv haruach, veten tal umatar) and the timing of when one begins and ends requesting rain

name: Anenu and Special Fast Day Prayers
notes: The twenty-four blessing prayer recited on fast days, including the six additional blessings with special conclusions invoking historical episodes of divine response

name: Ne'ila Prayer (Closing Prayer)
notes: The closing prayer recited on communal fast days and Yom Kippur, representing a fourth Amida in a single day alongside shacharit, musaf, and mincha

name: Ma'amadot (Non-Priestly Watches)
notes: The system of Israelite representatives parallel to the priestly watches who would stand by the daily offerings and read from Genesis in their towns; their fasting schedule and Torah reading portions

name: Wood Offering (Korban Etzim)
notes: The nine annual wood-offering days when specific families volunteered wood for the altar, treated as private semi-holidays with special observances

name: Seventeenth of Tammuz Fast
notes: The five calamities that occurred on the seventeenth of Tammuz including the breaking of the tablets, cessation of the daily offering, breach of Jerusalem walls, burning of a Torah scroll, and placement of an idol in the Sanctuary

name: Laws of Tisha B'Av (Prohibitions and Practices)
notes: Specific prohibitions of the Ninth of Av week and day: haircuts, laundering, two cooked dishes, meat and wine; the custom of overturning one's bed

name: Mourning Practices of the Month of Av
notes: Decreasing acts of rejoicing from Rosh Chodesh Av, including restrictions on building, planting, business, betrothals, and greetings

name: Tu b'Av Celebrations and Marriage Market
notes: The daughters of Jerusalem dancing in borrowed white garments in vineyards to attract marriage partners; the concept that borrowed garments were required to avoid embarrassing the poor

name: Megillat Ta'anit (Scroll of Fasts)
notes: The ancient scroll listing days on which fasting and eulogizing are prohibited; rules about fasting on the day before and after such days

name: Ashes on the Ark and Heads on Fast Days
hebrew: אפר על ראשי הנשיא ועל התיבה
notes: The ceremony of placing burnt ashes on the ark, on the head of the Nasi and deputy Nasi, and on everyone's heads as a sign of mourning during communal fast days

name: Sounding the Shofar on Fast Days
notes: Blowing the shofar (tekiah and teruah) during communal fast days as a cry to God; the procedure in the Temple context vs. outside; distinction from Rosh Hashanah shofar

name: Ḥoni HaMe'aggel and the Circle (Drawing a Circle for Prayer)
notes: The narrative of Ḥoni drawing a circle and refusing to move until rain fell; his exchange with Shimon ben Shetach; paradigm of the tzaddik whose prayers are answered

name: Completing a Fast After Rain Falls (Hashlamat HaTa'anit)
notes: Whether a community must complete a fast after the desired outcome (rain) arrives before or after midday/sunrise; the incident in Lod with Rabbi Tarfon

name: Priestly Watch Members and Fasting (Mishmar and Patrilineal Family)
notes: Rules governing when the mishmar and bet av members may fast during communal fast periods, their prohibition on drinking wine, and restrictions on haircuts and laundering

name: Communal Mourning Customs When Fasts Are Unanswered
notes: When all fasts have been exhausted without rain, the community adopts mourning-like practices: reducing business, building, planting, betrothals, marriages, and greetings

name: Local Calamities Requiring Immediate Fasting
hebrew: תענית על צרות פרטיות של עיר
notes: Calamities requiring immediate communal fast without waiting: blight, locusts, dangerous beasts, pestilence, sword, a city receiving no rain while surroundings did; criteria for pestilence

name: Crying Out for Help on Shabbat (Tza'akah beShabbat)
notes: Crying out to God or summoning help on Shabbat for emergencies such as siege, flood, or shipwreck; dispute about whether crying out differs from sounding the alarm
